title: Present Perfect
tagline: experience and news: have / has + past participle
why: The present perfect connects the past to now. You need it to talk about your experience, give news, and say how long something has lasted, for example in a job interview.
know: the form have / has + past participle, with irregular verbs: go → gone, see → seen, write → written
the time words ever, never, just, already, yet, for, since
understand: why a finished time (yesterday, in 2019, two days ago) needs the past simple
the difference between for (a length of time) and since (a starting point)
able: talk about your life experience: I've never tried skiing.
give news: I've just found a new job.
say how long: I've known her for ten years.
mistakes: Are you ever been to Mexico?
I have finished already my work.
use: life experience, with no time given: I've travelled to Peru twice.
news with a result now: I've lost my wallet, so I can't pay.
a situation from the past to now: We've lived in Mississauga for six years.
a time that isn't finished: I've had three coffees today.
signals: ever, never, just, already, yet, so far, recently, today, this week, for + a length of time, since + a starting point. Past simple instead: yesterday, last year, ago, in 2018, When...?
tip: No finished time with the present perfect. If you say when (yesterday, last week, two years ago), use the past simple: I've been to Halifax, but I went to Halifax in 2019.

pick.why: For life experience, use have + ever + past participle: Have you ever been to Vancouver?

pick.q: We ___ to Niagara Falls last summer.
pick.why: Last summer is a finished time, so use the past simple: We went.
Since 2015 = from then until now, so use the present perfect: has worked.

pick.q: I've known my best friend ___ twenty years.
pick.why: Twenty years is a length of time, so use for.

pick.q: They haven't replied to my message ___.
pick.why: Yet goes at the end of negatives and questions: They haven't replied yet.

pick.q: My son ___ his driving test. He's so happy!
pick.why: Just goes between has and the past participle: has just passed.
When asks about a finished time, so use the past simple: When did you come?

pick.q: He ___ a horse. He's afraid of them.
pick.why: Never goes after has, and the past participle of ride is ridden.

type.q: I ___ (already / send) the invoice to the client.
type.why: Already goes between have and the past participle: I have already sent.

type.q: My parents ___ (never / fly) in a plane.
type.why: Life experience: have + never + past participle. fly, flew, flown.
Yet = up to now, so use the present perfect: She hasn't finished.
Since 2018 = from then until now: We have lived (or have been living) here.
Last weekend is a finished time, so use the past simple: I saw.
How long + to now: have you known. Know is a state verb, so no -ing.

type.q: He ___ (just / break) his arm, so he's going to the hospital.
type.why: Recent news with a result now: has just broken. break, broke, broken.

type.q: I ___ (write) three emails so far this morning.
type.why: So far = up to now: I have written. write, wrote, written.

spot.q: I have met my wife in 2010.
spot.why: In 2010 is a finished time, so use the past simple: I met my wife in 2010.

spot.q: We have been married since twelve years.
spot.why: Twelve years is a length of time, so use for: We have been married for twelve years.

spot.q: He has wrote a book about his life.
spot.why: Use the past participle after has: write, wrote, written. He has written.
Since March = from then until now: I've worked here since March.

spot.q: Has she called you two days ago?
spot.why: Two days ago is a finished time, so use the past simple: Did she call you?

order.a: Have you ever been to the Rocky Mountains?
order.why: Have + you + ever + past participle: Have you ever been to the Rocky Mountains?

order.a: I haven't spoken to my brother since Christmas.
alt: Since Christmas I haven't spoken to my brother.
order.why: Haven't + past participle, with since + a starting point.

order.a: She has already booked the hotel for our trip.
order.why: Already goes between has and the past participle: has already booked.

order.a: How long have you had this car?
order.why: How long + have + you + past participle. Have (own) is a state verb.

pick.q: We ___ two meetings so far today.
pick.why: So far today = up to now, so use the present perfect: have had.

pick.q: My sister ___ to Mexico. She's coming back on Friday.
pick.why: Has gone = she is there now. Has been = she went and came back.

pick.q: They ___ each other since high school.
pick.why: Since high school = from then until now: have known.
With you, the present perfect uses have: Have you finished yet?

pick.q: He moved to Toronto three years ___.
pick.why: Ago goes with the past simple to say when: three years ago.

pick.q: I ___ to the gym since my operation.
pick.why: Since my operation = from then until now: I haven't been.

type.q: We ___ (not / decide) where to go on holiday yet.
type.why: Yet = up to now: We haven't decided.

type.q: My daughter ___ (just / start) a new job.
type.why: Recent news: has just started. Just goes before the past participle.
Last night is a finished time, so use the past simple: I lost.
Life experience to now: How many countries have you visited?

type.q: He ___ (be) a nurse for fifteen years. He loves it.
type.why: For fifteen years, and he still is: has been.
In 2016 is a finished time, so use the past simple: bought.
Experience: has + never + past participle. drive, drove, driven.

type.q: I ___ (already / pay) the bill, so we can go.
type.why: A result now (we can go): have already paid. pay, paid, paid.

spot.q: I have visited my aunt last Sunday.
spot.why: Last Sunday is a finished time, so use the past simple: I visited my aunt.
Has needs the past participle: He has finished his lunch.

spot.q: My parents has lived here for years.
spot.why: My parents = they, so use have: My parents have lived here for years.

spot.q: I didn't see her for a long time. I miss her.
spot.why: The time continues to now (I miss her): I haven't seen her for a long time.

order.a: Have you finished the report yet?
order.why: Have + you + past participle, with yet at the end.

order.a: We have just come back from Florida.
order.why: Just goes between have and the past participle: have just come.

order.a: I have never tried Korean food.
order.why: Never goes between have and the past participle: have never tried.

bank.q: Have you ___ the new manager yet?
bank.why: After have, use the past participle: Have you met the new manager yet?
Last week is a finished time, so use the past simple: I visited.
January is a starting point, so use since.
Ever goes before the past participle been: Have you ever been to Newfoundland?

bank.q: I ___ ten kilometres today and it's only noon.
bank.why: Today isn't finished yet, so use the present perfect: I have walked.
Ago goes with the past simple to say when: ten years ago.

bank.q: We ___ very little snow so far this winter.
bank.why: So far = up to now, so use the present perfect: have had.
Last night and What time? ask about a finished time: past simple. What time did you get home?

bank.q: My brother ___ (work) in that restaurant for six months now.
bank.why: For six months now = until now: has worked (or has been working).

bank.q: I ___ (not / see) that film yet. Is it good?
bank.why: Yet = up to now: I haven't seen it. see, saw, seen.

bank.q: How many times ___ (you / be) to Quebec City?
bank.why: Experience up to now: How many times have you been?

bank.q: Sorry, he isn't here. He ___ (just / leave).
bank.why: Recent news with a result (he isn't here): has just left. leave, left, left.

bank.q: We ___ (move) to this street when I was a child.
bank.why: When I was a child is a finished time, so use the past simple: moved.

bank.q: She has gone to the dentist yesterday.
bank.why: Yesterday is a finished time, so use the past simple: She went to the dentist yesterday.

bank.q: I have knew him for many years.
bank.why: Have needs the past participle: know, knew, known. I have known him for many years.

bank.q: Have you ever missed a flight?
bank.why: Correct! Life experience: Have you ever + past participle.

bank.q: We've lived in this apartment since 2021.
bank.why: Correct! Since 2021 = from then until now, so we've lived is right.

bank.a: Has your sister found a new apartment yet?
bank.why: Has + your sister + past participle, with yet at the end.

bank.a: I have already told you the answer.
bank.why: Already goes between have and the past participle: have already told.

bank.a: How long have you worked at the hospital?
bank.why: How long + have + you + past participle: How long have you worked there?
